title: Pluperfect and future perfect

objectives.can: Recognise pluperfect and future perfect indicatives.

explanation.summary: The pluperfect and the future perfect are built on the perfect stem you learned in the last lesson, with endings that look like the imperfect and the future of *sum*. They place an action before another time: before a past moment (pluperfect, 'had done') or before a future one (future perfect, 'will have done').

sections.heading: Relative time
body: The perfect, the pluperfect and the future perfect are the three tenses of completed action. They differ in the moment from which the action is seen as complete: the present for the perfect, a past moment for the pluperfect, a future moment for the future perfect.

In Matthew 26:75 Peter remembers a saying: *quod dixerat*, 'which he had said'. The saying came before the remembering, and the pluperfect says so. In John 11:13, *Dixerat autem Jesus de morte ejus* is 'now Jesus had spoken of his death': the reader is told this before the disciples' misunderstanding.

sections.heading: The pluperfect: perfect stem + -eram
body: The pluperfect is the perfect stem with the imperfect endings of *sum*: -eram, -eras, -erat, -eramus, -eratis, -erant. You find the stem by taking the third principal part and dropping -i: *dixi* gives dix-, and then *dixerat*; *feci* gives fec-, and *fecerat*. Because the perfect stem is used, the pluperfect of *video* is *viderat*, not *videbat*, which is the imperfect.

Latin uses the pluperfect to say 'had': a past action which was completed before another past action named or understood. It is common in the Gospels, where a narrator explains what had happened earlier, as in John 4:45, which says what Jesus *fecerat* in Jerusalem. English does not always keep the 'had': 'when he saw what he did' may translate a Latin pluperfect, where the order is clear.

sections.heading: The future perfect: perfect stem + -ero
body: The future perfect is the perfect stem with the future of *sum* (without the first -s-): -ero, -eris, -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint. It means 'will have done', and Latin uses it where English prefers a simple present: in a clause beginning with 'if' or 'when', Latin writes the future perfect when the action is completed first and the main verb is future. So in Luke 22:67, *Si vobis dixero, non credetis mihi* is 'if I tell you, you will not believe me', and in John 14:3 *si abiero et præparavero vobis locum* is 'if I go and prepare a place for you'. English says 'go' and 'prepare'; Latin says the going and the preparing will be completed before the coming.

The future perfect is much rarer than the other two. Its endings coincide in most persons with those of the perfect subjunctive (taught later): *-erit* and *-erint* are both. The first person singular -ero is different, so the analysed texts hold almost only first person singular forms that the analyser reads as certainly future perfect: *dixero*, *dedero*, *fecero*, *videro*, *habuero*, *potuero*. The other persons occur in Latin, but they are not asked in this lesson.

sections.heading: The three tenses of completed action
body: The same stem gives all three tenses. For each verb you need only one stem and the three sets of endings.
The forms of *sum* itself (*fuerat*, *fuerant*, *fuero*) are filed as an auxiliary verb in the analysis and so do not appear in this lesson's exercises.

misunderstandings: *viderat* (pluperfect, 'he had seen') and *videbat* (imperfect, 'he was seeing') are different tenses: the first is built on the perfect stem vid-, the second on the present stem vide- with -ba-.

The future perfect is not 'a future with a perfect meaning' in every English translation. In Latin 'if I say' about a future occasion is often *si dixero*, and English translations then use the simple present.
The 3rd person ending -erit does not by itself prove a future perfect. It is the same as the perfect subjunctive, and the sentence decides which it is.
The pluperfect and the future perfect are built on the perfect stem for every verb, so the -e- before -ram or -ro does not depend on the conjugation: *audierat* and *habuerat* both have -erat.

deeper.heading: Why -er- in both?
body: The -er- common to the pluperfect and the future perfect is generally explained as a form of *sum* attached to the perfect stem: -eram is the imperfect of *sum* and -ero its future, both with the first s changed to r between vowels. The details of the endings, and in particular how the future perfect came to look like the perfect subjunctive, are debated, so the account here is only one standard view.

examples.analysis: *Dixerat* is the pluperfect of *dico*, third person singular: 'he had spoken'. The stem dix- is that of the perfect *dixit*, and the ending is -erat. The narrator explains what Jesus had meant, and the pluperfect puts that explanation before the disciples' mistake. *putaverunt* ('they thought') is an ordinary perfect and carries the story forward.

examples.analysis: A perfect and a future perfect of the same verb. *dixi* is first person singular perfect: 'I have told'. *dixero* is first person singular future perfect: 'I shall have told', or in English 'if I tell'. The -ero ending gives the tense, and the clause belongs to a condition about the future.

examples.analysis: Two future perfects joined by *et*: *abiero* (from *abeo*) and *præparavero* (from *praeparo*). Both are first person singular in an 'if' clause. The coming back is future; the going and the preparing are completed before it, which is why Latin puts them in the future perfect. The English edition has 'if I shall go, and prepare'.
